answers.question: I haven't run for two weeks. Do I have to start again from the beginning? And is the 5K in four weeks still realistic?
answers.answer:
No, you do not have to start again. Two weeks off costs you a little sharpness, but you keep what you built since late August. Monday steps back one notch to 7 runs of 2 minutes, and Wednesday returns to your usual 8.

If Monday feels fine, you are back on track. If it feels much harder than effort 6/10, repeat it on Wednesday before moving on.

Finishing the 5K is realistic. Running the whole way is a stretch, and I would rather tell you now than on race morning.

So far your longest run without a walk is 2 minutes, and the race will take you around 40 to 45 minutes. Most beginners need about six more steady weeks to get from 2 minute runs to 30 minutes nonstop. You have three weeks of building plus a lighter race week.

Each week the running stretches will get longer, reaching about 8 to 10 minutes by early November. On race day you would run with short planned walk breaks, which is still a strong first 5K. If the next few weeks go smoothly with no gaps, we can look at the target again.

new.analysis:
## How the week went
You missed all three planned walk-runs this week, and you missed the week before as well. With your mum in hospital, that was the right call. Your last run was Sat Oct 3, so Monday will be 16 days since.

## What you still have
Before the break you were holding 2 minute runs at effort 6/10 with no pain. Your heart rate also settled as each session went on. That kind of fitness fades slowly, so a short step back is enough.

## Why the week looks like this
The week rebuilds before it builds. A big first session after a break is when aches and bad mornings tend to show up. Only once you are back at your usual level does the plan ask for more.

There are no fast sessions, even with the race close. For your goal, the race-specific work is running for longer without a break, not running faster. Every session stays easy.

## Slow down to go longer
Running slower is your best tool for running longer. Your running parts were around 7:40 per km, and on Sat Oct 3 that pushed your heart rate higher than it needs to be. Slow down until you could chat, even if it feels barely faster than walking.

## The real risk is another gap
Another missed fortnight is a bigger threat to race day than your fitness. If a morning falls through, move the session to the next day rather than skipping it or doubling up. Keep your Monday, Wednesday and Saturday routine whenever you can, because a steady rhythm is what gets the running stretches longer.

## Looking ahead
Over the next two weeks the plan builds your running stretches, and then race week eases off. We will settle your race-day pattern of running and walking in early November, based on how those weeks go.
